Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 24
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Tailor
  trauma_type: Life-threatening motor vehicle collision
  pcl5: 41

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat, Worst Case Rehearsal: mentally rehearse worst case scenarios to feel prepared, Avoid Driving: Driving or being a passenger in a vehicle
  Threat: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert, Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room, Scanning for Danger: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger
  Memory: Reliving Event: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now., Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over., Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
  Negative Appraisals: Constant Vigilance: I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next, Distrust Others: People are not what they seem, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Vignette:
Leila is a 24-year-old single woman who works as a tailor in a small shop in Dearborn, Michigan. She came to therapy at the urging of her aunt, who had grown worried about the changes in her niece over the past eight months. Eight months ago, Leila was driving home from work on a rainy November evening when a pickup truck ran a red light and T-boned her sedan at an intersection. The impact spun her car into a lamppost. She remembers the sound of metal crumpling, the shattering of the driver’s side window, and the sudden, suffocating pressure of the airbag against her chest. For what felt like an eternity, she was trapped, her door jammed shut, the smell of gasoline thick in the air. She was certain she was going to die, that the car would explode. A passerby pulled her out through the passenger window before the paramedics arrived. She walked away with a fractured wrist and deep bruising, but the physical injuries healed within weeks.

What did not heal was the feeling that the world had become a trap. Leila now lives in a state of constant, low-grade dread. She has come to believe that disaster can strike at any moment, without warning, and that the only way to survive is to be ready. She finds herself scanning every room she enters, her eyes darting to exits, to the faces of strangers, to any object that could become a weapon or a hazard. At the tailor shop, where she spends her days bent over sewing machines and fitting clients, she cannot focus. Every time a car backfires outside or a door slams, her heart lurches and she feels the same terror she felt in the crushed car. She has taken to positioning her worktable so that her back is against the wall, facing the door. She feels unsafe any other way. Her boss has noticed she jumps at the bell on the shop door, and her coworkers have stopped trying to startle her as a joke—they learned quickly that she would react with a scream and trembling hands.

The worst part of the day is the drive home. Leila has not driven since the accident. She cannot bring herself to get behind the wheel. The mere thought of sitting in a driver’s seat, of approaching an intersection, sends her into a panic. She relies on her aunt for rides, or she takes the bus, but being a passenger is almost as bad. Every time the vehicle slows down, she braces for impact. She mentally rehearses the worst-case scenario: the truck coming from the left, the sound, the crushing feeling. She does this to feel prepared, as if rehearsing the horror might somehow make it less likely to happen, or at least make her ready for it. But it only keeps the event fresh. Her memories of the crash are not static; they are vivid, intrusive, and replay in her mind like a film she cannot turn off. When she remembers it, she is back inside the car, her chest tight, the smell of gasoline in her nostrils, the absolute certainty that she is about to die. The terror is identical to what she felt that night.

Her social life has shrunk. She used to meet friends for coffee, but now she avoids it. She cannot trust that people are what they seem. She looks at strangers and wonders what they are capable of. The world, she has concluded, is a fundamentally dangerous place, and she has to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next. She has difficulty falling asleep because she feels she needs to stay alert, as if letting her guard down for a moment would invite catastrophe. She lies awake, listening to the sounds of her apartment building, her muscles tense.

What finally brought her to seek help was a moment at work last week. A client’s child, playing near the front window, suddenly slammed a toy car against the glass. Leila screamed, dropped the fabric she was cutting, and began to cry uncontrollably. She could not stop shaking for an hour. Her aunt, who works at the shop part-time, took her aside and told her she could not keep living like this. Leila agreed to come to therapy, but she is not sure it will help. What she fears most is that this feeling of being hunted will never go away, that she will spend the rest of her life bracing for the next disaster. What she hopes for, though she can barely admit it, is to one day sit in a car without her heart racing, and to feel, even for a moment, that she is safe.
